questions.question: What is the main performance downside of a fully controlled form with one useState per field?
options: It can't validate input at all
Every keystroke in any field re-renders the entire form component
It only works with class components
It can't submit data to a server
questions.explanation: Each controlled input's onChange updates state, triggering a re-render of the whole form on every keystroke — fine for small forms, costly for large ones.

questions.question: How does React Hook Form avoid re-rendering the form on every keystroke?
options: It disables the browser's input events
It keeps inputs uncontrolled, reading their values via refs instead of state, and only re-renders on submit or validation
It requires inputs to be read-only
questions.explanation: register() wires an input via ref rather than controlled state, so typing doesn't trigger a React re-render of the form.

questions.question: What advantage does centralizing validation in a Zod schema give you over inline rules like `{ required: true, pattern: /.../ }`?
options: It makes the form submit faster over the network
A single schema can be reused for both client-side validation and a server-side check, avoiding duplicated validation logic
It removes the need for a submit button
It's required for React Hook Form to work at all
questions.explanation: A Zod schema is just a plain object describing the shape and constraints of the data — the same schema can validate a Server Action's input, not just the client form.

questions.question: What does `zodResolver` do when passed to `useForm({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) })`?
options: It converts the form into a Server Action automatically
It plugs the Zod schema's validation into React Hook Form's error state, so `errors` is populated from the schema
It styles the form according to the schema
It disables all built-in HTML validation attributes
questions.explanation: The resolver bridges Zod's schema validation results into React Hook Form's formState.errors object automatically.
